chunks: How a sample is held steady. The question: How the the sample voltage maintained throughout the entire sample duration?
A sample is held on a capacitor, and a capacitor keeps its voltage only if its charge has nowhere to go.
In real circuits a tiny leakage current always drains it, so the voltage slowly sags. That sag is called droop.
Holding a sample steady means making every leak path very small, and keeping the hold short.
Picture a bucket with a tiny hole. The water level is the voltage, and the water that drips out is the leakage. With a small hole, the level falls slowly.
A wider bucket falls even more slowly for the same hole, which is why a bigger capacitor droops less. Heat makes the hole bigger: leakage roughly doubles every 10 degrees.
Droop grows linearly with time, with slope I over C .
At the default 10 picofarads, the half-LSB line is crossed at 40 microseconds for 100 pA, 4 microseconds for 1 nanoamps and 0. 4 microseconds for 10 nanoamps.
Anything with microsecond conversion times lives comfortably at 1 nanoamps; a 10 nanoamps leak (a hot switch, or a bipolar-input buffer) fails.
Drag C down to 1 picofarads: droop becomes ten times faster, and even 100 pA crosses the half-LSB line after about 4 microseconds.
Hold capacitor: ("What capacitance is"): the capacitor that stores the sampled voltage. Leakage current: a tiny unwanted current that slowly drains the capacitor.
Droop: the slow fall of the held voltage because of leakage. Buffer amplifier: an amplifier that reads the held voltage while drawing almost no current.
LSB: ("How an ADC works"): the size of one step of the ADC.
The droop rate is the leakage current divided by the capacitance. Take 1 nanoamps of leakage on a 10 picofarads capacitor.
That is 1 nanoamps / 10 picofarads = 100 volts per second, which is 0. 1 millivolts per microsecond. A conversion that takes about 1 microseconds loses about 0.
1 millivolts, well under one 12-bit step of about 0. 8 millivolts. Hold the sample for 100 microseconds, though, and the loss is 10 millivolts, about 12 steps.
That is the whole idea.
"The sample is stored as charge on a capacitor.
When the switch opens, the capacitor has nowhere to dump that charge, as long as the switch is highly off and the next stage is a high-impedance buffer like a MOSFET input.
What remains is leakage, which gives droop dV over dt equals I leak over C : 1 nanoamps on 10 picofarads is 0. 1 millivolts per microsecond.
To keep it steady I use a bigger capacitor, low-leakage switches and buffers, a short hold time, and on the board, guard rings.
Leakage doubles about every 10 degrees, so hot is the worst case."
